scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: Hello IT, the partner connection keeps HICCUPING --
pc2 (200.1.1.2) drops out on me every so often and feels slow in between (I'm
on pc1). The link between our border router and theirs is obviously FLAPPING
-- it keeps going down and up, down and up, you can practically hear it!!
Please reset the connection between the two border routers and make it stay
up for more than five minutes!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I investigated the eBGP interconnect between the two border routers (router1:eth0 193.10.11.1 ↔ router2:eth0 193.10.11.2). The BGP session is currently Established on both sides and exchanging one IPv4 prefix each (show bgp summary on both routers). Interface health looks clean: router1:eth0 and router2:eth0 are UP/LOWER_UP with no RX/TX errors or drops (ip -s link), and ethtool reports link detected, full duplex. Queueing stats (tc -s qdisc) on all participating interfaces (routers and hosts) show no drops or ECN marks.

End-to-end data and control-plane checks are stable. From pc1 to pc2, large 1400-byte pings over 50 probes show 0% loss and sub‑2 ms RTTs. iperf from pc1→pc2 sustains ~148 Mb/s; there was one brief retransmission burst, consistent with transient TCP congestion, not with a link or routing flap. The only BGP anomaly seen was a single early reset during initial neighbor bring-up (router1 shows 1 Notification sent and “Last reset ~1m45s ago”), after which keepalives and updates have been steady.

Localization: No evidence of link flaps on router1:eth0 or router2:eth0, and no route churn in FRR. Mechanism: the ticket likely observed the initial BGP convergence/reset shortly after services started, not an ongoing flap. Root cause: transient BGP OPEN/negotiation issue at startup. Corrective fix: no change needed. If faster/livelier detection is desired, consider enabling BFD on the eBGP peering and disable verbose BGP debugging to reduce log noise. I recommend monitoring the BGP neighbor uptime; it should remain stable beyond five minutes.
